skill_drafts.name: Dynamic Timestamp Allocation (DTA) for Deadlock Detection
skill_drafts.description: A timestamp-based technique for detecting and resolving deadlocks in 2PL algorithms. Timestamps are associated with transactions and compared when conflicts occur to identify and prevent circular wait conditions. Provides foundational understanding of pessimistic concurrency control mechanisms and their scalability trade-offs.
applicable_signals: Need for deadlock detection in pessimistic locking schemes
Requirement to understand timestamp-based conflict resolution
Architectural decision point between 2PL and OCC
contraindications: Optimistic concurrency control (OCC) is the primary method
Tuple-level timestamp tracking is required (DTA uses transaction-level timestamps only)
Systems requiring sub-16-thread scalability with shared global resources
triggers: Comparing pessimistic vs. optimistic concurrency control approaches
constraints: DTA timestamps are transaction-level, not tuple-level
Shared global resources in implementations create critical section bottlenecks
Scalability degrades significantly beyond 16–32 active threads
cautions: DTA OCC implementations with considerable critical section logic fail to scale as expected
Do not confuse DTA timestamp association (transaction-level) with TicToc tuple-level timestamp tracking
output_contract: Documented understanding of DTA mechanism, its dependency graph analysis approach, and empirically observed scalability limitations (critical section bottleneck beyond 16–32 threads). Caller receives reference knowledge sufficient to evaluate DTA as a deadlock prevention strategy and understand why it may not scale in high-contention scenarios.

examples.input: Architect is choosing between 2PL with DTA and OCC for a transaction system with medium contention
examples.output: Reference knowledge that DTA uses transaction-level timestamps and dependency graphs for deadlock detection, but implementations with shared global resources scale poorly beyond 16–32 threads; OCC may be preferable if scalability is critical
examples.notes: Supports architectural decision-making by clarifying DTA's known bottleneck

metadata.prompt: DTA associates timestamps with each transaction and compares them when two transactions conflict. Use dependency graph analysis to detect circular dependencies that indicate deadlocks. Be aware that implementations with shared global resources (critical sections) typically fail to scale beyond 16–32 active threads due to contention bottlenecks.

skill_drafts.name: OCC Critical Section Bottleneck Detection
skill_drafts.description: A diagnostic safety rule identifying when optimistic concurrency control (OCC) implementations fail to scale due to shared global resource contention in the critical section. Detects scaling plateaus and confirms bottleneck root cause.
applicable_signals: OCC implementation shows performance degradation with increasing core count
Scaling plateau observed between 16–32 active threads
Shared global state present in critical section (locks, atomic operations, synchronized structures)
contraindications: Using lock-free or fully distributed algorithms without global synchronization points
Critical section already eliminated or redesigned to avoid shared state
Single-threaded or low-contention workloads where scaling is not a concern
intervention_moves: Inspect critical section code for shared global resources (locks, atomic counters, synchronized data structures)
Measure critical section execution time and contention rate across thread counts
Compare performance with and without critical section to isolate its impact
triggers: OCC implementation shows performance degradation; core count exceeds 20; shared global state is present in critical section
constraints: Requires multi-core benchmarking environment with measurable thread scaling
Workload must exhibit sufficient contention to trigger critical section bottleneck
Measurement must isolate critical section overhead from other performance factors
cautions: Scaling plateau may be masked by other bottlenecks (memory, I/O); isolate critical section impact before concluding
Threshold range (16–32 threads) is empirical; actual plateau point varies by hardware and implementation
output_contract: Identification of scaling plateau point and confirmation that bottleneck is global resource contention in the critical section, not algorithm logic or other factors. Output includes core count at which scaling fails and evidence of shared global state causing contention.

metadata.prompt: When benchmarking OCC performance, monitor scaling behavior across increasing core counts. If performance plateaus or degrades significantly between 16–32 active threads, inspect the critical section for shared global state (locks, atomic operations, or synchronized data structures). Confirm that the bottleneck is global resource contention rather than algorithm logic by isolating critical section overhead.
